title: Die Scholle
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 172. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (daß, Fluthen). This tale is mostly in High German, but the flounder's taunting cry is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 172 is a short just-so story: the fish, tired of swimming without order, hold a race to choose a king, and the flounder — who has fallen far behind — sneers at the herring for finishing first. Ever since, the tale says, the flounder has had a crooked mouth as punishment for its envy: a brief dip into Low German dialect within an otherwise High German telling.

sentences.t: Die Fische waren schon lange unzufrieden daß keine Ordnung in ihrem Reich herrschte.
sentences.l: The fishes had long been discontented that no order prevailed in their realm.
sentences.i: The fishes had long been unhappy that no order reigned in their realm.
sentences.n: “daß” is the 1857 spelling of modern “dass”; the conjunction ‘that’ introduces the cause of their discontent.

sentences.t: Keiner kehrte sich an den andern, schwamm rechts und links, wie es ihm einfiel, fuhr zwischen denen durch, die zusammenbleiben wollten, oder sperrte ihnen den Weg,
sentences.l: None troubled himself about the other, swam right and left, as it occurred to him, drove through between those that wished to stay together, or barred them the way,
sentences.i: No one paid any heed to the next, swam this way and that as the whim took him, cut in between those that wanted to keep together, or blocked their path,
sentences.n: “sich an jemand kehren” is an old idiom, ‘to concern oneself with someone’; negated here, none cared about the others. “wie es ihm einfiel” — literally ‘as it fell into his mind,’ i.e. as he pleased.

sentences.t: und der stärkere gab dem schwächeren einen Schlag mit dem Schwanz, daß er weit weg fuhr, oder er verschlang ihn ohne weiteres.
sentences.l: and the stronger one gave the weaker one a blow with the tail, so that he shot far away, or he swallowed him without more ado.
sentences.i: and the stronger would give the weaker a blow with its tail, so that it shot far off, or else swallowed it outright.
sentences.n: Comparative adjectives used as nouns: “der stärkere” / “dem schwächeren” = ‘the stronger / the weaker one.’ “ohne weiteres” — without further ado, just like that.

sentences.t: „Wie schön wäre es, wenn wir einen König hätten, der Recht und Gerechtigkeit bei uns übte“ sagten sie,
sentences.l: “How fine it would be, if we had a king who exercised right and justice among us,” said they,
sentences.i: “How fine it would be if we had a king to keep right and justice among us,” they said,
sentences.n: The wish stands wholly in the subjunctive: “wäre … hätten … übte.” “Recht und Gerechtigkeit üben” — to administer law and justice.

sentences.t: und vereinigten sich den zu ihrem Herren zu wählen, der am schnellsten die Fluthen durchstreichen und dem Schwachen Hilfe bringen könnte.
sentences.l: and agreed together to choose for their lord the one who could sweep through the waters fastest and bring the weak one help.
sentences.i: and agreed to choose as their lord whichever of them could sweep through the waters fastest and bring help to the weak.
sentences.n: “wählen” here is High German ‘to choose, elect’ — not the Low German ‘wollen’ (to want) that the same spelling marks elsewhere in the corpus. “Fluthen” is the 1857 spelling of ‘Fluten’ (waters, tides).

sentences.t: Sie stellten sich also am Ufer in Reihe und Glied auf, und der Hecht gab mit dem Schwanz ein Zeichen, worauf sie alle zusammen aufbrachen.
sentences.l: So they drew themselves up on the bank in rank and file, and the pike gave a sign with his tail, whereupon they all set out together.
sentences.i: So they lined up on the bank in rank and file, and the pike gave a signal with its tail, whereupon they all set off together.
sentences.n: “sich aufstellen” — to line up, take position; separable, the particle “auf” lands at the end. “in Reihe und Glied” is a fixed phrase, ‘in rank and file.’

sentences.t: Wie ein Pfeil schoß der Hecht dahin und mit ihm der Hering, der Gründling, der Barsch, die Karpfe, und wie sie alle heißen.
sentences.l: Like an arrow the pike shot along, and with him the herring, the gudgeon, the perch, the carp, and whatever they all are called.
sentences.i: Like an arrow the pike shot off, and with it the herring, the gudgeon, the perch, the carp, and whatever else they are all called.
sentences.n: “und wie sie alle heißen” — ‘and however they are all named,’ a storyteller’s shrug at the long list of fish.

sentences.t: Auch die Scholle schwamm mit und hoffte das Ziel zu erreichen.
sentences.l: The flounder too swam along and hoped to reach the goal.
sentences.n: “die Scholle” — the flounder (or plaice), the flat-fish this tale is about; “mitschwimmen” = to swim along with the rest.

sentences.t: Auf einmal ertönte der Ruf „der Hering ist vor! der Hering ist vor.“
sentences.l: All at once the cry rang out, “the herring is ahead! the herring is ahead.”
sentences.i: All at once the cry rang out, “the herring’s in front! the herring’s in front.”
sentences.n: “vor” here is High German ‘in front, ahead’ (short for ‘vorn’). Note how the flounder answers with the Low German “vör” in the next line.

sentences.t: „Wen is vör?“ schrie verdrießlich die platte mißgünstige Scholle, die weit zurückgeblieben war, „wen is vör?“
sentences.l: “Who is in front?” cried peevishly the flat, envious flounder, who had stayed far behind, “who is in front?”
sentences.i: “Who’s in front?” the flat, envious flounder cried peevishly, having been left far behind, “who’s in front?”
sentences.n: Low German in the flounder’s mouth: “wen” = wer (who), “is” = ist (is), “vör” = vorn (in front). The narration stays High German; only the fishes ‘speak’ dialect.

sentences.t: „Der Hering, der Hering“ war die Antwort.
sentences.l: “The herring, the herring” was the answer.
sentences.n: A bare naming answer — ‘the herring’ stands as the whole reported reply, with “war die Antwort” carrying it.

sentences.t: „De nackte Hiering?“ rief die neidische, „de nackte Hiering?“
sentences.l: “The bare herring?” cried the envious one, “the bare herring?”
sentences.i: “That bare herring?” the envious one cried, “that bare herring?”
sentences.n: More Low German: “de” = der (the), “Hiering” = Hering (herring). “nackt” (bare, naked) is a sneer at the plain, undistinguished herring — and the envy is what earns the flounder its punishment.

sentences.t: Seit der Zeit steht der Scholle zur Strafe das Maul schief.
sentences.l: Since that time the flounder’s mouth stands crooked, for a punishment.
sentences.i: Ever since, the flounder’s mouth has stood crooked as a punishment.
sentences.n: Dative of possession: “der Scholle … das Maul” — literally ‘to the flounder the mouth,’ i.e. the flounder’s mouth. “zur Strafe” = as a punishment.

glossary.wählen: wählen — to choose, elect (infinitive; High German, NOT the Low German ‘wollen’ = to want that this spelling marks elsewhere)
